**The Weight of a Thousand Words**

The first word is always the heaviest. It sits on your tongue like a stone, reluctant to be spoken. The second word is lighter, but still hesitant, as if testing the air before committing. By the third word, you’re in motion, and the rest spill out like water from a broken dam—uncontrolled, inevitable.

I’ve always been fascinated by words. Not just their meanings, but their weight, their texture, the way they shape the world around us. A single word can build a bridge or burn it down. It can heal or wound. It can be a whisper or a scream.

I remember the first time I realized the power of words. I was ten years old, sitting in my grandmother’s kitchen, watching her hands move deftly over a bowl of dough. She was teaching me how to make bread, but she was also teaching me something else—something far more important.

“Words are like flour,” she said, pressing her palms into the dough. “You can’t see them, but they’re in everything. And just like flour, if you don’t measure them carefully, they can ruin the whole thing.”

I didn’t understand then, but I do now. Words are the invisible ingredients of life. They shape our thoughts, our relationships, our very sense of self. They can be nourishing, like a warm loaf of bread, or they can be toxic, like spoiled milk.

I’ve spent my life collecting words—hoarding them like a dragon with its treasure. I’ve written them down in journals, scribbled them on napkins, whispered them into the night. Some words are sharp, like the edge of a knife. Others are soft, like a blanket on a cold night. But all of them, in their own way, have shaped me.

There are words I regret. Words I wish I could take back, like arrows I’ve already loosed. There are words I’ve never said, buried deep in my chest, too afraid to let them out. And then there are the words I’ve spoken without thinking, the ones that linger in the air long after I’ve forgotten them.

I’ve written love letters and hate letters. I’ve written poems that made me cry and stories that made me laugh. I’ve written words that changed lives and words that meant nothing at all. But no matter what I write, no matter how many words I use, I always feel like I’m falling short.

A thousand words. That’s what you asked for. A thousand words, and I still don’t know what to say. Maybe that’s the point. Maybe the weight of a thousand words isn’t in their meaning, but in their absence. Maybe the most powerful words are the ones we never speak.

But for now, I’ll keep writing. Because even if I never find the right words, the act of searching for them is enough. It keeps me moving forward, one word at a time.

And that’s all any of us can do.
